title: Inserting Data From Queries
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of inserting data from queries.
Apply insert into ... select in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn inserting data from queries through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Inserting Data From Queries matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use inserting data from queries to make database structure and data rules explicit. Preview changes, name constraints deliberately, consider dependencies, and keep schema evolution in versioned, reviewable scripts.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: INSERT INTO ... SELECT, Copying data between tables, Inserting aggregated results, Inserting filtered data. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: INSERT INTO ... SELECT
items.text: INSERT INTO ... SELECT changes stored data. Preview the target rows, specify a restrictive predicate where appropriate, validate constraints, and wrap related changes in a transaction that can be reviewed before commit.

items.title: Copying data between tables
items.text: Copying data between tables helps you insert, update, delete, synchronize, and return changed data safely, using bounded changes, staging, conflict handling, and transactions where needed. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Inserting aggregated results
items.text: Inserting aggregated results summarizes rows. Decide the grain of the result first, group only by the dimensions that define one output row, and verify NULL and duplicate behavior in each metric.

items.title: Inserting filtered data
items.text: Inserting filtered data changes stored data. Preview the target rows, specify a restrictive predicate where appropriate, validate constraints, and wrap related changes in a transaction that can be reviewed before commit.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

content.task: Try it yourself: demonstrate inserting data from queries using the sample schema. State what each returned row represents, test one edge case related to the lesson, and record the result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic insert into ... select and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
